indicators.note: the father goes round, so his word encloses the female's word

parts.note: dad is an informal word for father
she is the female pronoun

explanation.surface: A woman's father holds her together when she is distraught.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shattered' at the start looks like a description of the woman, but it is the definition, meaning dejected; 'gets ... round' is the containment signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Hopes that are dashed have been ruined, the same as broken or wrecked.

explanation.surface: Two short instructions: cut down, and press the laundry.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is a pun: ironing takes the creases out, so it de-creases a garment.
explanation.definitionFit: To dwindle is to grow smaller; ironing removes wrinkles, read playfully as un-creasing.

clue.text: Car tested, found faulty, broken up

indicators.note: a car found faulty at its test has something wrong, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A car fails its roadworthiness test and is sent for scrap.
explanation.definitionFit: Things dispersed in all directions have been split apart and spread around.

parts.note: Eve is a woman's name, the first woman in Genesis

explanation.surface: Someone insists that a name is a woman's one after all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'still' is the adverb of 'still more' or 'yet', not 'motionless'.
explanation.definitionFit: Used for emphasis, as in 'better yet', the word means yet or all the more.

clue.text: These days an alternative to fostering

definitions.text: These days an alternative to fostering

parts.note: AD, anno Domini, marks the present era
an option is a choice or alternative

explanation.surface: Nowadays, taking a child in permanently is a common choice instead of temporary care.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines the answer while also building it from its pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Taking a child permanently into a family is the legal route beside short-term foster care.

parts.note: not ceremonial troops but older women in Spain who protected a young lady's reputation

explanation.surface: Ceremonial troops lining a parade route in Madrid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Guards of honour' suggests soldiers; here it means chaperones guarding a girl's honour.
explanation.definitionFit: A Spanish chaperone watched over unmarried young women to protect their good name.

clue.text: Place might turn out to be dull and lifeless

indicators.note: letters that turn out differently are rearranged into a new order

explanation.surface: A town may prove boring and dead once you get there.
explanation.definitionFit: A stolid, unemotional temperament is slow to rouse, apathetic and sluggish.

clue.text: In the meantime, I'm off to Bury!

indicators.note: the word I'm is to come off, taken away from the longer word

parts.note: interim means the meantime or temporary
taken as written, without its apostrophe

explanation.surface: Someone announces a short trip to the Lancashire town of Bury.
explanation.walkthrough: Bury is a town near Manchester, but here it is the verb. 'off' removes IM from INTERIM.
explanation.definitionFit: To bury a body is to lay it in a grave, which is what this verb says.

clue.text: Fancied to win and made a pile

explanation.surface: A tipped horse wins and its backer cleans up.
explanation.walkthrough: A racing tipster's 'nap' is the day's best bet; fabric's nap is its raised pile.
explanation.definitionFit: A horse given as a tipster's strongest selection; cloth whose fibres have been raised into a soft surface.

parts.note: a precious metal in a pirate hoard, and also the surname of the pirate in Treasure Island

explanation.surface: What a buccaneer keeps in his chest.
explanation.walkthrough: Long John is the pirate in Stevenson's Treasure Island; the metal is also loot.
explanation.definitionFit: A precious metal found in pirate hoards shares its name with Stevenson's one-legged buccaneer.

clue.text: Unusually fierce sea battle ends with it

indicators.note: the words are set out in an unusual order, so their letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A ferocious naval engagement is finally halted.
explanation.definitionFit: A truce halting the shooting is how fighting comes to a stop.

parts.note: a pause or slackening, pictured as releasing something pressed down

explanation.surface: Advice to stop pushing so hard on something.
explanation.walkthrough: A pause in effort is pictured literally as allowing something pressed down to rise.
explanation.definitionFit: A slackening or pause in effort is a relaxation of intensity.

indicators.note: a recipe is a formula for mixing, so the letters are combined anew

explanation.surface: Someone dines on a fixed menu dish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'recipe' is read as a mix of ingredients, the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To devour food is to take it in, which is what the verb means.

clue.text: Innovative advantage involved in capturing king

indicators.note: the jumbled letters capture the king, holding him inside
involved means intricate or tangled, so the letters are mixed

parts.note: R, from Latin rex, abbreviates king

explanation.surface: A chess player turns an edge into checkmate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'involved' scrambles ADVANTAGE to AVANTGADE, and 'capturing' puts R inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Pioneering, experimental art leads the way ahead of fashion.

clue.text: Learn a craft? He's bound to

definitions.text: Learn a craft? He's bound to

parts.words: Learn a craft? He's bound to
parts.note: a trainee legally tied by indentures to a master in order to learn a trade

explanation.surface: Someone sure to pick up a skill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bound to' seems to mean 'certain to', but refers to being bound by indentures.
explanation.definitionFit: A trainee serving under a skilled master was formally contracted to learn the trade.

clue.text: A poor fiddler outside the door

explanation.surface: A busker with a violin plays on the doorstep.
explanation.walkthrough: A bad violinist scrapes the bow; a boot scraper sits by the front door to clean mud off shoes.
explanation.definitionFit: An unskilled violinist sawing at strings; a metal blade by the doorstep for cleaning boots.

clue.text: Is suffering a setback, internally affected by seafood

indicators.note: one piece goes inside the other, held internally
a setback sends the word back, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: camp means theatrical or affected in manner

explanation.surface: Someone falls ill after eating dodgy shellfish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'suffering a setback' turns the clue's own word round to SI; 'affected' is not illness but camp, a theatrical manner.
explanation.definitionFit: Breaded langoustine tails are a familiar shellfish dish.

clue.text: Point of the joke in periodical row

parts.note: Punch was a long-running British humorous magazine
a line is a row

explanation.surface: A gag's climax appears in a magazine's column.
explanation.walkthrough: Punch was a British satirical weekly, apt in a clue about jokes.
explanation.definitionFit: The final line of a gag carries its humour, its pay-off.

parts.note: a sure winner, read literally as a certainty that is lifeless

explanation.surface: A gloomy tipster says no horse is guaranteed to win.
explanation.walkthrough: A sure-thing racing bet starts with a word for lifeless, so no living horse can be one.
explanation.definitionFit: A racing term for a horse sure to win, a guaranteed thing.

parts.note: to do someone is to swindle or cheat them
a blushing face is red

explanation.surface: A lover catches a deceitful partner going pink.
explanation.definitionFit: Worshipped or cherished deeply; doted on.

explanation.surface: Sort things out so as to throw them away.
explanation.walkthrough: To dispose troops is to arrange them; to dispose of rubbish is to discard it.
explanation.definitionFit: Placing items in order; discarding what is unwanted.

clue.text: Dressed up, goes in with sweetheart, looking elegant

indicators.note: letters dressed up are put in a new arrangement

parts.note: the heart of the word sweet is its middle letter

explanation.surface: Someone dresses smartly to call on a lover.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dressed up' rearranges GOES IN into SOIGNE; 'sweetheart' gives the middle letter of 'sweet'.
explanation.definitionFit: Well-groomed and sophisticated, a French loan for someone smartly turned out.

parts.note: not a shared investment but a pointed rod pushed through meat

explanation.surface: A shared share in a business.
explanation.walkthrough: 'joint stake' suggests co-ownership; it is a pin through a joint of meat.
explanation.definitionFit: A long pin piercing meat for roasting is a stake through a cut.

parts.note: alludes to the idiom telling chatterers to stop talking

explanation.surface: An order to stop and shut up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut the ...' is a British idiom meaning stop the idle chatter and get to the point.
explanation.definitionFit: Noisy chatter or a hen's clucking, which the idiom tells you to cut.

parts.note: a puff is a promotional plug, an ad
to doctor is to treat, and to minister to the sick is to tend them

explanation.surface: Someone breathless from running needs medical help.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Run' seems physical, but means manage. 'doctor' is the verb: to tend or treat.
explanation.definitionFit: To manage an organisation is to direct or control its affairs.

parts.note: the mean is an average
T as in T-shirt

explanation.surface: An ordinary shirt is called for.
explanation.definitionFit: Signified or intended; what a sign signified.

explanation.surface: Throwing something into the garden hut.
explanation.definitionFit: Cast off, as a snake does skin; a simple garden hut.

parts.note: WA abbreviates Washington, a US state
providing means if, on condition that

explanation.surface: The government supporting street children.
explanation.definitionFit: A stray, neglected youngster with no home.

parts.note: habit as clothing: the drab uniform cloth a British soldier put on

explanation.surface: A man named Tommy picked up a bad routine.
explanation.walkthrough: Tommy, or Tommy Atkins, is slang for a British private; 'habit' means dress, not routine.
explanation.definitionFit: Dull brownish-yellow cloth used for army uniforms.

clue.text: Prove a tie looks odd for a manual worker

indicators.note: letters that look odd are out of order, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone shows that his necktie seems peculiar.
explanation.definitionFit: A factory hand or mechanic doing physical labour.

parts.note: not stingy gratuities but the far ends of a range, which are never the average

explanation.surface: Generous gratuities.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tips' suggests gratuities and 'mean' stinginess; really ends of a range, never the average.
explanation.definitionFit: The furthest ends of a scale, its utmost limits.

explanation.surface: Faking it in order to sway people.
explanation.definitionFit: To feign an air; to act upon or change something.
